coreTruths.title: Implant success rests on osseointegration: a direct titanium-to-bone bond with no soft tissue layer in between
coreTruths.broaderContext: Implants work because titanium fuses directly with bone. Lose that bond and the fixture becomes a foreign body. Everything in implantology serves protecting it.
coreTruths.body:
## Osseointegration is a direct, load-bearing bond, not a soft tissue interface

Osseointegration means the titanium fixture is locked straight into bone, with no connective tissue layer in between [1]. That direct bond is what lets an implant carry occlusal load. Almost every modern implant is titanium because nothing else has matched it for predictable integration [2]. The roughened surface, by grit-blasting, acid etching, or coating, is there to give bone more surface area to grab onto [3].

## Healing is time-dependent and easily wrecked by premature loading

Integration is a slow biological process: blood clot, granulation tissue, woven bone, then lamellar bone over weeks to months. Conventional loading sits at 2 to 6 months and is still the gold standard [4]. Load too early or too hard and the bone never gets there. Connective tissue fills the gap instead, and the implant fails to integrate [5]. Bone necrosis from drilling without irrigation does the same thing for a different reason [6], so constant cooling matters.

## Failure splits into early (no integration) and late (lost integration)

1 degree failure is failure to integrate in the first place: bad site prep, overheated bone, infection, premature loading, or no primary stability [7]. 2 degree failure is losing integration after it was achieved, mostly from overloading or peri-implantitis [7]. Knowing which type is happening shapes the rescue plan, and most late failures trace back to peri-implantitis [8].

citations.quote: Implantology in restorative dentistry is based on the principle of osseointegration, i.e. a direct functional and structural connection between a load-carrying titanium implant with bone, with no intervening connective tissue.

Many materials and coatings for implants have been used in the past (e.g. ceramics and hydroxyapatite) but success rates have been found to be greatest with titanium fixtures. As a result, almost all modern implants are titanium.

Modern implants usually have a roughened outer surface to ↑ the surface area for integration. The surface may be roughened by a subtractive technique such as being grit-blasted (e.g. with titanium dioxide) and/or acid-etched. Additive techniques can also be used such as coating with hydroxyapatite or a fluoride-modified surface.
Traditionally the time from placement to integration and loading has been accepted as 2–6 months. In certain circumstances, implants may be loaded earlier than this, even immediately.

However, there are few indications for this and if the implant is prematurely loaded or overloaded during the healing phase, there may be connective tissue encapsulation of the implant body, preventing osseointegration.
Careful technique with constant irrigation is required to avoid overheating bone resulting in bone necrosis.

Early failure may be due to inadequate site preparation, overheating of bone, infection, premature loading, or lack of 1° stability. Late failure may be due to overloading or infection (peri-implantitis).
The majority of implant failures are due to peri-implantitis.

coreTruths.title: Implant planning is prosthetically driven: the crown decides where the fixture goes, not the bone
coreTruths.broaderContext: An integrated implant in the wrong place is a clinical failure. Top-down planning starts from the final tooth position, then asks whether the bone allows it.
coreTruths.body:
## Plan the tooth first, the fixture second

The planning approach is top-down or prosthetically driven. The final tooth position gets decided first, on wax-ups or digitally, and the implant gets positioned to serve that restoration [1]. A successfully integrated implant in the wrong place is still a failure [2]. The wax-up turns into a radiographic stent and often the surgical guide too, so what was planned on the bench actually ends up in the bone [3].

## Bone has to fit around the planned position, not the other way round

Minimum spacing rules drive a lot of decisions. Leave 1.5 mm or more between implant and adjacent teeth, so a single 4 mm fixture needs at least 7 mm of mesiodistal space, and 3 mm between adjacent implants [4]. If the bone will not allow the planned position, the choice is augmentation or a different prosthetic option [4], not a compromised implant.

## CBCT earns its dose when 3D anatomy actually changes the plan

Plain films give height; CBCT gives volume in three dimensions and lets the planning software produce surgical guides [3]. The trade-off is extra radiation [3], so it is not the default. It is justified when the position of the inferior alveolar nerve, mental nerve, antrum, or adjacent roots could change the plan [5].

## Augmentation timing matters and assessment ideally happens before extraction

When there is enough bone for primary stability and soft tissue closure, augmentation can run alongside placement. If not, it goes first, with 3 to 6 months of healing before the implant [6]. The longer the wait between extraction and augmentation, the more bone resorbs, so implant assessment ideally happens before the tooth comes out [6].

citations.quote: This uses the ‘top-down’ or ‘prosthetically driven’ approach. This means deciding on tooth position by first using wax-ups on mounted study models, or digitally.
There is little point in a successfully integrated implant in the wrong place!

The wax-up can be used to produce a radiographic stent which is used to help plan the appropriate size and position of the implant. Further radiographs may be indicated with the stent in position such as a CBCT scan. CT scanning has the advantage over plain film radiography of allowing a 3-D assessment of the bone volume. This radiographic stent can often also be converted into a surgical stent to help guide implant placement. Digital implant planning systems (e.g. SimPlant®) are now available. These allow for 3-D planning and the production of surgical guides. A disadvantage of CBCT scanning is an additional patient dose of radiation.

When planning implants, 1.5mm or more is left between the implant and adjacent teeth. So, for a single tooth implant the minimum space between adjacent teeth is 7mm for a 4mm diameter fixture; 3mm of space is usually required between adjacent implants. If there is insufficient bone available to allow correct implant positioning, then either bone augmentation is required or other prosthetic options need to be considered.
Moderate- to high-risk structures include the inferior alveolar nerve, mental nerve, lingual nerve, and sublingual/submental arteries.

It may be feasible to simultaneously carry out bone augmentation at the time of implant placement if there is sufficient bone to allow 1° stability of the implant fixture and soft tissue closure. Alternatively, the bone may need to be augmented prior to implant placement and allowed to heal (for 3–6 months) before the implant can be placed, known as a two-stage approach. The later bone augmentation procedures are performed after tooth extraction, the more bone resorption will occur, therefore timing of such procedures should be planned carefully and implant assessment should take place before extraction of a tooth where possible.

coreTruths.title: Peri-implant tissues are biologically weaker than periodontal tissues, so plaque control around an implant is non-negotiable
coreTruths.broaderContext: Peri-implant mucosa has fewer fibroblasts and less blood supply than gingiva. It cannot fight plaque the way real gum can, which is why peri-implantitis is the leading cause of late failure.
coreTruths.body:
## Peri-implant mucosa is structurally weaker than gingiva

The soft tissue collar around an implant looks like gum but does not behave like it. It is poor in fibroblasts, rich in collagen fibres, and has a limited blood supply, so it has a lower potential for repair than gingival tissue [1]. That structural weakness is the reason routine plaque control matters more around an implant than around a tooth.

## Peri-implant mucositis is reversible, peri-implantitis is not

Peri-implant mucositis is reversible inflammation of the soft tissue with no bone loss, the implant analogue of gingivitis [2]. Peri-implantitis is destructive inflammation that has reached bone, the analogue of periodontitis [3]. Catching it at the mucositis stage is the whole game, because once the bone is gone, it is gone. Despite a 90 percent plus 10 year survival, more than 40 percent of patients experience peri-implantitis to some extent [3].

## Risk factors are mostly the periodontal ones plus a few implant-specific traps

Increased risk lines up with poor OH, prosthesis designs that hinder OH, excessive occlusal load, poorly controlled diabetes, existing periodontal disease (treated or not), smoking, thin bone coverage at placement, residual cement from cemented restorations, and thin gingival biotype [4]. Patients with treated periodontitis are slightly more susceptible to peri-implantitis, implant failure, and peri-implant bone loss [5], so a periodontitis history is not a green light to proceed without thinking. Cement left subgingivally is a particularly avoidable cause of peri-implant disease [6].

## Maintenance is part of the treatment, not optional aftercare

If implants survive the first 2 years, success runs at 98 percent with dramatic functional gains [7]. That number assumes ongoing maintenance, both home care and clinical follow-up, with regular radiographs to spot bone loss [7]. Diagnosis of peri-implantitis is radiographic bone loss plus tissue colour and bleeding changes, suppuration, and increased probing depths [8]. Management ranges from local debridement and OH improvement to surgery with bone grafts and regenerative procedures [8].

citations.quote: Peri-implant mucosa—soft tissue healing surrounding the implant after placement establishes the peri-implant mucosa. The outermost surface of the peri-implant mucosa is pink, firm, and covered by keratinized epithelium. It is poor in fibroblasts, rich in collagen fibres, and has a limited blood supply, and thus has a lower potential for repair than gingival tissue.
Peri-implant mucositis is a condition of reversible inflammation of the soft tissue around an implant but which does not show any peri-implant bone loss (similar to gingivitis around teeth).

Peri-implantitis is a condition with destructive inflammation of the soft and hard tissues surrounding an osseointegrated implant (similar to periodontitis around teeth). Although implants have a 90%+ chance of 10yr survival, >40% of patients may experience peri-implantitis to some extent.

Peri-implantitis and peri-implant bone loss is not well-understood but ↑ risk is associated with:
Inadequate OH.
Prosthesis designs that hinder OH.
An excessive occlusal load on the implant.
Poorly controlled diabetes.
Existing periodontal disease (treated and untreated).
Smoking.
Thin bone coverage at the time of implant placement.
Residual cement from a cemented implant restoration.
Thin gingival biotype and tissue thickness.
Active periodontal disease or history of treated periodontitis (slightly more susceptible to peri-implantitis, implant failure, and peri-implant bone loss).
Fig. 9.3 Peri-implant disease due to cement left below the gingival margin.

If implants survive the first 2yrs, there is a 98% success rate with dramatic improvement in all functional parameters. Success rates for the mandible are higher than those for the maxilla (due to bone quality). Implant-retained restorations need to be carefully maintained by the patient. The implant needs to be followed up long term clinically and radiographically by the clinician.

Diagnosis involves radiographic examination to look for bone loss around the implant, assessment of the gingival tissue (colour and bleeding), evidence of suppuration, and ↑ probing depth of peri-implant pockets. Management can range from local debridement and improved OH to surgery with bone grafts and regenerative procedures.

coreTruths.title: Implants succeed or fail on case selection, not just surgical skill
coreTruths.broaderContext: Most implant failures are predictable from the consultation. Host factors, habits, and expectations decide outcomes more reliably than the brand of fixture or the surgeon's hand.
coreTruths.body:
## Not every missing tooth needs an implant

While attractive to many patients, not all teeth need replacing and case selection drives appropriate treatment [1]. The shortened dental arch concept, premolar to premolar in both arches, is a practical and cost-effective alternative for many patients [2]. Every consultation should run through the full prosthetic menu (no treatment, removable partial denture, fixed bridge, or implant) and include all of it in the consent process [3].

## The relative contraindications are mostly about healing and host risk

The contraindications are not surgical, they are biological. Smoking, poorly controlled diabetes, anticoagulation, active chemotherapy, past or present jaw radiotherapy, immunocompromise, and bisphosphonate or denosumab use (IV greater than oral) all sit on the list [4]. Active or treated periodontitis adds risk too, because those patients are slightly more susceptible to peri-implantitis, implant failure, and peri-implant bone loss [5]. Poor plaque control alone is a relative contraindication [4]. None of those are absolute, but each one needs to be on the table before signing consent.

## Unrealistic expectations are as disqualifying as bad bone

Unrealistic patient expectations and an unfavourable smile line are explicit relative contraindications [4]. Patients vary in what they need to feel functional and confident, so the consultation has to dig into expectations and motives before anyone reaches for a wax-up [6]. Many patients will pay more for an implant than a denture and accept the cost, but only when the trade-off has actually been talked through [6].

## Risk consent is broader than peri-implantitis

The consent conversation has to cover pain, swelling and bruising, bleeding, failure to integrate, peri-implantitis, nerve damage, sinus problems, damage to adjacent teeth, infection, implant or abutment screw fracture, gingival recession, prosthesis problems, and rarely mandible fracture or bony necrosis [7]. Bony necrosis is a specific risk in patients with a history of radiotherapy or bisphosphonate use [7]. Naming these up front is what makes consent meaningful when something goes wrong years later.

citations.quote: However, while an attractive option to many patients, not all teeth need replacing and case selection is important to ensure appropriate treatment provision.

The shortened dental arch (SDA) concept1 is advocated by many dentists due to its practicality and cost-effectiveness. This is defined as reduced dentition with missing posterior teeth and remaining intact anterior teeth, i.e. pre-molar to premolar in both arches.
All prosthetic options (i.e. no treatment, removable partial denture, fixed bridge, or implant) should be considered and, if appropriate, included in the consent process.

Relative contraindications for implants
Poor plaque control.
Poor bone quality or soft tissue biotype.
Smoking.
Anticoagulation therapy.
Active chemotherapy.
Alcohol or drug abuse.
Radiotherapy to the jaw bones (past or present).
Diabetes (particularly if poorly controlled).
Unfavourable smile line.
Unrealistic patient expectations.
Oral medicine conditions may compromise healing.
Cardiac conditions considered high risk for infective endocarditis.
Chronic kidney disease (healing impairment).
Immunocompromised (transplant patients, AIDS/HIV).
Medications predisposing to medication-associated osteonecrosis, such as denosumab or bisphosphonate use (past or present, risk IV > oral).
Active periodontal disease or history of treated periodontitis (slightly more susceptible to peri-implantitis, implant failure, and peri-implant bone loss).

What is acceptable to one patient may not be acceptable to another and therefore an in-depth consultation involving discussion of the patient’s expectations and motives for wanting implant treatment is paramount. In general, a high number of patients are willing to pay more for implants than conventional dentures and accept the difference in cost.

Risks include:
Pain, swelling, and bruising.
Bleeding.
Failure to osseointegrate and lack of stability.
Peri-implantitis and late failure.
Bony necrosis in patients with a history of radiotherapy or bisphosphonate use.
Nerve damage.
Sinus problems (due to protrusion of implant into sinus).
Accidental damage to adjacent teeth and structures.
Very rarely, mandible fracture and necrosis of surrounding flap tissue.
Infection (including peri-implantitis and peri-implant mucositis) (Fig. 9.3).
Implant fracture.
Gingival recession.
Broken, loosened, worn, or discoloured prosthesis.
Fracture of abutment screw or implant.
